originalGoal.statement: Owner can leave the computer for long periods while TSF continues useful, bounded engineering work without drifting from the original goal, across seven upgrades that turn TSF into a real daily-driver planner/autonomy layer over Orca.
sevenUpgrades: M1: Project Onboarding V1 -- Add Project -> Analyze -> Health -> Direction -> Upgrade Backlog -> Known/Active/Work Set
M2: Keep Going / Overnight V1 -- real project-level long-run controller over Orca (highest priority)
M3: Chat -> Dispatch + Live Work Feed -- Planner Chat becomes operational, not just conversational
M4: Run Journal + Recovery -- durable run timeline, restart recovery, no repeated settled work
M5: Capacity-Aware Routing -- route around provider capacity without manual meter-watching
M6: Desktop TSF -- double-click launch, no manual localhost/terminal management
M7: Project Memory V2 -- durable selective memory (facts/decisions/preferences/lessons) across planner sessions
approvedExtensions: M8: Project Estimator + Delivery Planner -- approved by Tim 2026-08-19T21:48 as an addition beyond this original seven, not a change to it. See milestones[] -> M8 for the full research/harvest plan. Explicitly not started; execution order after M7 unless Tim says otherwise.

waves.summary: Genuine independent verification pass: launched the code-review skill (effort 'high') as a forked, separately-reasoning execution over the full M2 diff (tsf/main...HEAD, 22 files, ~3450 insertions) -- the first real VERIFIER_INDEPENDENT-style pass on this milestone's cumulative work, not SELF. It returned 6 findings, all triaged and addressed honestly rather than dismissed:

reviewFindings.summary: raiseNeedsYou generated an id as sha256({question, taskId, at}) with no uniqueness guard; two identical questions raised in the same clock tick (guaranteed under a fixed/mocked clock) would collide, permanently stranding the older entry as unresolvable and locking the run in NEEDS_YOU forever.
reviewFindings.verdict: CONFIRMED real bug
reviewFindings.fix: Added an insertion-ordinal (next.needsYou.length) to the hash input in tsf/domain/keep-going.mjs. Regression test added in keep-going.test.mjs proving two identical-content questions get distinct ids and both resolve cleanly.

reviewFindings.summary: startKeepGoingRun/pauseKeepGoingRun/resumeKeepGoingRun did read-modify-write on persisted operator state with no optimistic-concurrency check, even though the run already carries a revision field and the codebase has an established assertExpectedRevision pattern (mission-state.mjs, adoption.mjs) for exactly this. Two concurrent requests for the same project could silently lose a transition.
reviewFindings.verdict: CONFIRMED real bug
reviewFindings.fix: Added expectedRevision support to keep-going.mjs's transitionRun (and thus pauseRun/resumeRun), matching mission-state.mjs's transitionMission pattern exactly (assertExpectedRevision from canonical.mjs, optional param, backward compatible). Threaded expectedRevision through keep-going-controller.mjs, keep-going-http-routes.mjs (now returns 409 TSF_STALE_REVISION on conflict, not 422), api.ts, and KeepGoingPanel.tsx (sends run.revision on every pause/resume). Domain-level, controller-level, and HTTP-level regression tests added; browser-confirmed the happy path still works transparently.

reviewFindings.summary: StartForm never collected a budget value even though this program's own wave-6 state.json entry claimed the UI closes the acceptance criterion 'literally (goal/Usage Mode/budget/constraints/stop conditions... all present and real)' -- an overclaim in the program's own durable record, not just a missing feature.
reviewFindings.verdict: CONFIRMED real bug + overclaim in prior wave's own narrative
reviewFindings.fix: Added real maxWaves/maxRetriesPerTask/maxConcurrentWorkers/stallThresholdMs inputs to StartForm (defaulting to keep-going.mjs's own DEFAULT_BUDGET), sent as a real budget object to POST start, and displayed on LiveRun. Browser-confirmed the defaults render and a started run carries them.

reviewFindings.summary: mapOrchestrationFacts always emits lastHeartbeatAt: null (no real timestamp exists in worker-list output today, by design -- see wave 3), so detectStall (Date.parse(null) => NaN) can never flag a real worker as stalled once this projection is wired into a live run.
reviewFindings.verdict: PLAUSIBLE, already disclosed
reviewFindings.fix: No code change -- there is no real timestamp source to use without fabricating one, which the program discipline explicitly forbids. Already documented as a known limitation in the wave-3/wave-4 code comments and state.json entries; strengthened nothing further tonight but leaving this exact limitation as a recorded, open gap rather than silently accepting it as resolved.

reviewFindings.summary: keep-going.mjs implements its own independent Run-level state machine instead of importing/composing mission-state.mjs or coordinator.mjs, contradicting docs/tsf/M2_KEEP_GOING_DESIGN_V1.md's explicit prose claim that it 'composes mission-state.mjs/coordinator.mjs (one Mission per wave) rather than reimplementing mission lifecycle' -- a real documentation-accuracy bug, and adjacent to the charter's 'no competing foundation' concern.
reviewFindings.verdict: CONFIRMED documentation inaccuracy
reviewFindings.fix: Corrected the module header comment in tsf/domain/keep-going.mjs to state plainly that it is a distinct Run-level state machine one level above the per-wave Mission lifecycle, does not import mission-state.mjs/coordinator.mjs today, and that the design doc's 'one Mission per wave' language describes the intended future wiring for the not-yet-built autonomous wave-dispatch loop, not existing code. docs/tsf/M2_KEEP_GOING_DESIGN_V1.md itself is flagged as needing the same correction -- recorded as a remaining gap rather than edited tonight, to keep this wave bounded.

reviewFindings.summary: KeepGoingPanel only rendered StartForm when run.started === false, so a run that reached BLOCKED or COMPLETE had no way to start a new run from the UI even though startKeepGoingRun's own guard explicitly permits starting fresh after either state.
reviewFindings.verdict: CONFIRMED real UX bug
reviewFindings.fix: Added a 'Start a new run' button on LiveRun when state is COMPLETE or BLOCKED, toggling KeepGoingPanel back to StartForm. Verified by code inspection (small, low-risk conditional render) plus typecheck; not separately browser-driven tonight since reaching BLOCKED/COMPLETE isn't reachable through the UI yet (no dispatch loop).

Of the 5 findings, 1 was fixed, 1 documented as a real remaining gap without a quick fix available, 2 are legitimate architectural critiques deliberately not addressed (too large for the remaining runway), and all recorded honestly below rather than silently dropped.

reviewFindings.summary: startKeepGoingRun (the route that creates rather than transitions a run) had no expectedRevision check at all, even after wave 7 added it to pause/resume -- two concurrent 'start a new run after COMPLETE/BLOCKED' requests could silently overwrite each other, the exact race wave 7 was supposed to close everywhere.
reviewFindings.verdict: CONFIRMED real bug, wave 7 gap left open
reviewFindings.fix: Added expectedRevision support to startKeepGoingRun (checked via assertExpectedRevision only when a prior COMPLETE/BLOCKED run exists -- a brand-new first run has nothing to be stale against), threaded through keep-going-http-routes.mjs (start route now also returns 409 TSF_STALE_REVISION), api.ts, and KeepGoingPanel.tsx (the 'Start a new run' flow now sends the finished run's revision). Controller-level regression test added (start-after-COMPLETE race); full suite + lint/format/typecheck/build all GREEN.

reviewFindings.summary: raiseNeedsYou's already-NEEDS_YOU early-return branch and resolveNeedsYou's still-open early-return branch both mutate run state directly without going through transitionRun -- neither bumps run.revision nor accepts/checks expectedRevision, unlike every other mutation path in the module.
reviewFindings.verdict: CONFIRMED real inconsistency, currently zero live exposure (neither function is wired to an HTTP route yet -- confirmed by the reviewer's own grep)
reviewFindings.fix: Not fixed tonight. Real correctness debt in not-yet-exposed code; lower urgency than finding 1 (which was live). Recorded as an explicit gap for whoever wires raiseNeedsYou/resolveNeedsYou to a route (the autonomous wave-dispatch loop's eventual job) to fix at that time, not silently inherited as if it were already safe.

reviewFindings.summary: The keep-going-http-routes.mjs extraction (wave 7, forced by http-server.mjs's max-lines cap) reads as a one-off workaround rather than a generalized pattern -- the file now has two inconsistent conventions for HTTP routes (inline vs. one bespoke extracted module), and the comparably-sized onboarding route block was left inline, so the same problem will recur.
reviewFindings.verdict: PLAUSIBLE, legitimate architectural critique, not a bug
reviewFindings.fix: Not addressed -- generalizing to a real router abstraction across all of http-server.mjs's route groups is a genuine refactor, not a bounded fix, and explicitly the kind of new-architecture-surface work this evening-sprint window should not start close to the cutoff. Recorded as a real piece of debt for a dedicated future pass, not hidden.

reviewFindings.summary: assertExpectedRevision only guards the keepGoingRun sub-object; saveState() still does a blind whole-document overwrite of all of opState (chatThreads, portfolio, onboardedProjects, fixtureReceipts, usageMode, etc.), so two concurrent requests touching different unrelated slices of opState can still silently drop one write.
reviewFindings.verdict: PLAUSIBLE, legitimate architectural gap, not a bug in this wave's own scope
reviewFindings.fix: Not addressed -- general document-level optimistic concurrency across data-store.mjs would touch every feature that reads/writes opState, a substantially larger undertaking than this wave's bounded scope of 'protect the keepGoingRun field specifically.' Recorded honestly: tonight's fix narrows one specific race, it does not generalize to whole-document safety.

Session recovery: prior terminal was closed after the RETURN_HANDOFF checkpoint (commit a255f5321); resumed cleanly with HEAD/tree matching that checkpoint exactly, tsf/main HEAD unchanged (dirty working tree there is the same pre-existing external-session pattern as CONCURRENT-SESSION-DIRTY-TSF-MAIN-001, not this program), no orphaned orchestration workers or terminals belonging to this program, Codex CLI healthy (`codex doctor` 0 fail, `codex --version` 0.148.0 -- confirms the sandbox-crash incident did not recur), 136/136 baseline suite GREEN before starting. Implemented: (1) tsf/domain/keep-going.mjs gains inFlightWave tracking plus dispatchWave/settleInFlightWave (a wave is recorded as 'out for real work' before it settles, so a crash between dispatch and settle is recoverable, not lost or double-counted); (2) tsf/adapters/orca-orchestration-bridge.mjs gains listOrchestrationTasks (task-list is the correct settlement-polling surface per wave 11's own dogfood finding that worker-list only tracks worker-start-launched workers, not dispatch-into-existing-terminal tasks); (3) new tsf/server/keep-going-dispatch-loop.mjs (tickKeepGoingRun) performs one bounded plan+dispatch-or-settle step per call, idempotent and safe to invoke repeatedly, honoring expectedRevision like every other real mutation path in this codebase. Deliberately NOT done, disclosed rather than glossed over: (a) no independent verification -- Orca reporting a task 'completed' is the worker's own claim, so this loop never marks an acceptance criterion verifiedSatisfied from that alone (would violate Section F's 'no worker self-report treated as done'); (b) no candidate-work-item generation -- deciding what work items exist for the current gap remains a caller-supplied planning judgment; (c) no registered `orca automations create --trigger cron` job yet -- that is a separate decision with its own interval/safety tradeoffs, not made unilaterally by this wave; the function is reachable today only by direct call (proven via dependency-injected orchestration fakes in tests, not live dispatch).

reviewFindings.summary: A freshly-created real Orca orchestration Run was silently dropped (never persisted) when the first task-create in a wave failed, so a new one got created and leaked on every retrying tick.

reviewFindings.summary: The expectedRevision check on tickKeepGoingRun only compares run.revision to itself across the tick's several awaited CLI round-trips, so it cannot catch a concurrent write landing on the same in-memory run mid-tick -- the module's own comment overstated what this protects against.
reviewFindings.verdict: CONFIRMED as described, but the same already-disclosed architectural gap as wave 8 finding 4 / wave 11 findings 1/6 (per-request atomic read-check-write in data-store.mjs and its routes), not a new bug
reviewFindings.fix: Corrected the comment to state precisely what the check does and does not protect against, rather than re-attempting the already-deferred larger architectural fix in this bounded pass.

reviewFindings.summary: settleStep never invoked the existing detectStall/markStalled watchdog, so a task status that never reaches a terminal state (cancelled, hung) left the wave WAVE_STILL_IN_FLIGHT forever with no escalation.
reviewFindings.verdict: CONFIRMED real gap
reviewFindings.fix: settleStep now escalates the run to STALLED via markStalled once the wave has been in flight longer than budget.stallThresholdMs, using inFlightWave.dispatchedAt (a real wall-clock timestamp this module already has) rather than the still-unavailable per-worker heartbeat (wave 11 finding 4's limitation is unchanged -- not newly solved). Regression tests added for both past-threshold (STALLED) and within-threshold (still WAVE_STILL_IN_FLIGHT) cases.

reviewFindings.summary: Hitting the per-task retry budget only produced a reported action (WAVE_SETTLED_RETRY_BUDGET_EXCEEDED); nothing stopped the same work item from being re-dispatched and re-breaching the budget on every subsequent tick.
reviewFindings.verdict: CONFIRMED real gap
reviewFindings.fix: settleStep now raises a real NEEDS_YOU question (via the existing raiseNeedsYou) instead, transitioning the run so it actually stops and an operator sees it rather than silently spinning. Action renamed WAVE_SETTLED_NEEDS_YOU; regression test updated and strengthened to assert run.state and the question text.

reviewFindings.summary: planWave's conflict-aware batching intends independent items to run in parallel, but dispatchStep still dispatches every item within a batch sequentially, multiplying wall-clock dispatch latency by batch size.
reviewFindings.verdict: PLAUSIBLE, legitimate efficiency gap, not a correctness bug
reviewFindings.fix: Not fixed this pass -- documented in-code as a deliberate deferral. Correctly handling partial failure among concurrently-dispatched items needs more care than the current sequential-with-early-return shape, and this bounded pass prioritized the correctness findings above it.

reviewFindings.summary: dispatchWave/settleInFlightWave checked their own in-flight invariant before assertExpectedRevision, so a stale-revision caller got TSF_WAVE_ALREADY_IN_FLIGHT/TSF_NO_IN_FLIGHT_WAVE instead of TSF_STALE_REVISION -- inconsistent with every other mutation in tsf/domain/keep-going.mjs, which all check revision first.

reviewFindings.fix: Reordered both functions to check assertExpectedRevision first. Regression test added proving a stale-revision caller gets TSF_STALE_REVISION even when the invariant would also fail, and that a correctly-revisioned caller still gets the real invariant error.

waves.summary: Tim-directed bounded concurrency hardening wave, prioritized above further dogfood: closed wave 15b finding 2 (the revision guard did not protect against state changing mid-tick) for real, rather than merely disclosing it again. Smallest safe model chosen per Tim's explicit preference: a claim/commit lock built on one small synchronous compare-and-swap primitive (tsf/server/keep-going-run-store.mjs, ~30 lines, wrapping data-store.mjs's synchronous loadState/saveState with no await in between -- the actual source of atomicity, not the revision check alone), not a broad data-store.mjs rewrite. tsf/domain/keep-going.mjs gains tickLock + claimTick/releaseTick (a tick claims exclusive ownership BEFORE any real CLI work, which is what prevents two ticks from both starting real duplicate dispatch -- an end-of-tick-only revision check cannot prevent that, since by the time either tick reaches its own check both may already have created real duplicate Orca tasks) and transitionRun now rejects external pause/resume/markStalled/raiseNeedsYou while a tick holds the lock (TSF_TICK_IN_PROGRESS), with a tickInternal bypass for the tick's own in-progress escalations. tsf/server/keep-going-dispatch-loop.mjs was restructured from a pure opState-in/opState-out function (which cannot enforce atomicity across its own awaits by construction) into one that owns its claim/commit against an injectable store. A commit that loses the CAS race (lock recovered as abandoned by another tick) reports a *_LOST_LOCK result honestly, surfacing any real orchestrationRunId/dispatchRecords it created for future reconciliation, rather than silently discarding or retrying unboundedly -- disclosed, not auto-healed, consistent with program discipline. See docs/tsf/M2_KEEP_GOING_DESIGN_V1.md's wave 16 section for full detail.

waves.adversarialTestsDelivered: tsf/test/keep-going-dispatch-loop-concurrency.test.mjs (new, 6 tests, real synchronous data-store.mjs backing, not a fake): two DISPATCH ticks racing (second rejected before touching orchestration, no duplicate task-create); two SETTLE ticks racing an already-in-flight wave (second rejected, worker result processed exactly once); a pause request arriving while a tick holds the lock (rejected, persisted state unchanged, then verified to succeed once the lock clears); a full tick completing correctly despite a concurrent pause attempt being rejected mid-flight; a tick that loses its lock to abandonment-recovery after creating real Orca resources (its stale commit throws TSF_STALE_REVISION, persisted state remains exactly what the winning tick established, the loser's orphaned resources are surfaced in its result rather than silently lost); tickKeepGoingRun's own *_LOST_LOCK result path exercised end to end. Plus tsf/test/keep-going.test.mjs: claimTick/releaseTick lifecycle, ACTIVE-only + revision-first checks, abandoned-lock timeout recovery, transitionRun's lock rejection + tickInternal bypass for pause/markStalled/raiseNeedsYou. Plus tsf/test/keep-going-dispatch-loop.test.mjs rewritten for the new (projectId, candidateWorkItems, clock, { orchestration, store }) signature, including a same-process two-overlapping-ticks test.

Also not attempted: automatic reconciliation/adoption of a losing tick's orphaned real Orca resources onto the winning tick's run (disclosed limitation, not a broad rewrite). Sequential-within-batch dispatch (wave 15b finding 5) remains correctly deferred.

waves.summary: Independent verification of wave 16, the Tim-required gate before dogfood: a forked code-review pass (effort high) on the wave 16 diff returned 6 findings, 2 of them genuine critical bugs IN the hardening itself (not just polish), all fixed the same session. Finding 1 (CRITICAL): the SETTLE-side commit closures (WAVE_SETTLED/WAVE_SETTLED_NEEDS_YOU) never actually checked the claim-time revision -- recordTaskAttempt's first call used the freshly-read run's own revision as its own expectedRevision, a tautology that can never detect the lock was recovered by another tick since the claim (the DISPATCH-side commit had correctly threaded claimed.revision; the SETTLE side had not). Finding 2 (CRITICAL): the WAVE_STALLED path's markStalled call had no expectedRevision parameter at all (zero protection), and tickInternal:true bypassed the lock check unconditionally regardless of whose lock was held. Both fixed by introducing commitClaimed, one shared wrapper every commit path now goes through that always hands the claim-time revision to the caller's mutateFn explicitly, plus adding expectedRevision to markStalled. Finding 3: TICK_LOCK_TIMEOUT_MS (fixed 2 minutes) could legitimately be exceeded by a real, healthy dispatch of many sequential work items -- fixed by storing the effective timeout on the lock itself, scaled by wave size at claim time. Finding 4: keep-going-http-routes.mjs's start/pause/resume routes still captured opState before await readBody(req) (wave 11 finding 1, left deliberately deferred in wave 16) -- meaning the tick's pause-rejection guarantee was only true for a caller already using keep-going-run-store.mjs directly, not over the actual HTTP route; fixed by routing all three mutating routes through withKeepGoingRun (reusing the existing pure controller functions unchanged via a throwaway single-project opState wrapper), closing wave 11 finding 1 for these three routes for real. Finding 5 (test coverage gap): the only abandoned-lock-recovery adversarial test exercised the DISPATCH path, not SETTLE/STALLED, which is exactly where findings 1/2 hid -- closed with two new mirrored real-store-backed tests (both would have failed against the pre-fix code) plus a new HTTP-level test proving pause is rejected over the real route while a tick holds the lock. Finding 6 (maintainability): addressed by the same commitClaimed consolidation that fixed findings 1/2.

waves.summary: Independent verification of wave 18: a forked code-review pass (effort high) on the wave 18 diff returned 5 findings, 2 of them genuine confirmed bugs in the new function, fixed the same session. Finding 1 (CONFIRMED): the NEEDS_YOU escalation on retry-budget exhaustion assumed the run could always legally reach NEEDS_YOU, but RUN_ALLOWED forbids it from PAUSED/BLOCKED/COMPLETE -- since pauseRun never checks inFlightWave, a run can genuinely be PAUSED with a real stalled wave, and calling abandonStalledWave on it would have thrown TSF_INVALID_RUN_TRANSITION from inside raiseNeedsYou, discarding the already-computed settlement/checkpoint (worse than the recovery this function was meant to replace). Fixed by checking RUN_ALLOWED[next.state] first; when illegal, records the fact in a checkpoint (RETRY_BUDGET_EXCEEDED_ESCALATION_SKIPPED) instead, preserving the honest settlement either way. Finding 2 (CONFIRMED): the in-flight-wave requirement was checked BEFORE the tick-lock check, the reverse of transitionRun's established order and this function's own doc comment -- a tick that claimed the lock but hadn't dispatched yet (inFlightWave still null) would make a concurrent call report the wrong error class (TSF_NO_IN_FLIGHT_WAVE instead of TSF_TICK_IN_PROGRESS), the exact bug class wave 15b finding 6 already fixed once elsewhere in this module, reintroduced here in reverse. Reordered to match. Finding 3 (real, minor): a stale tickLock object was left on the run after recovery even though isTickLockActive correctly treated it as inactive -- fixed by clearing it explicitly (safe, since reaching that point already proved inactivity). Finding 4 (disclosed, deliberately deferred): the retry-budget-consumption loop duplicates the near-identical one in keep-going-dispatch-loop.mjs's settleStep -- a real DRY concern, not a bug; not extracted into a shared helper this pass since it would mean touching keep-going-dispatch-loop.mjs a third time this session (already through two rounds of critical-bug fixes) for a maintainability improvement, judged not worth the added risk this late in an unattended session. Finding 5 (fixed): the function's header comment was multi-paragraph, against AGENTS.md's concise-comments rule -- trimmed to four lines.

waves.summary: ROOT CAUSE FOUND AND REPAIR PROVEN GREEN for blockers.ORCA_DISPATCH_INJECT_NOT_DELIVERING_001, under Tim's explicit overnight repair authorization. Read-only investigation of Orca's own bundled `orchestration` skill guide (`orca skills get orchestration --full`) revealed the exact answer: `dispatch --inject` is documented as the LOW-LEVEL path ('remain valid recipes for custom argv or topology that worker-start does not express'), while `orchestration worker-start` is documented as 'the normal supervised path' that 'composes the existing worktree, terminal, readiness, and dispatch primitives' and 'exits 0 only for ready' with real stage/failedStage/effects/residualResources diagnostics on failure. dispatch-show on both wave-17 failed dispatches confirmed the diagnosis precisely: contract_version 1, launch_token_hash present, but last_heartbeat_at: null and failure_count: 0 on both -- the dispatch was accepted at the CLI level but the target agent never engaged with it, with zero diagnostic signal from the --inject path itself. VERDICT: this is TSF adapter misuse (the wrong Orca-native primitive was chosen for real automated dispatch), NOT an Orca defect, NOT a version issue, NOT a Codex-terminal problem -- Orca's own documentation already named the correct, preferred alternative. Implemented startOrchestrationWorker + showOrchestrationWorker in tsf/adapters/orca-orchestration-bridge.mjs (wrapping worker-start/worker-show), stub-CLI tested first. Then ran ONE tiny, disposable, real live proof per Tim's required step 4: a fresh orchestration Run + Task ('create PROOF_WORKER_START.md containing one line') dispatched via worker-start into the EXISTING low-risk dogfood worktree with a FRESH agent terminal -- result: stage input_accepted, terminal effect created+accepted immediately (unlike --inject's silent zero-signal dispatch); Codex visibly engaged within seconds ('I'm using the Orca CLI skill because this dispatched task requires reporting completion through the coordinator's orchestration channel'); a real worker_done message arrived ~1m27s later (outcome succeeded, filesModified listed); INDEPENDENTLY verified (not trusting the worker's own claim) by reading the real file on disk (exact expected content, 22 bytes) and confirming task-list auto-transitioned to status completed; git status showed only the one expected untracked file, no unintended changes; worker-show confirmed state succeeded/stage settled; cleanly released via worker-release (terminal closed, transcript archived) and the disposable proof file deleted. All required proof points from Tim's step 4 met: task text reached Codex, Codex performed the exact bounded action, TSF observed real task state, settlement was recognized and attributable to the exact task/dispatch id, no duplicate worker/run, no sandbox/Access-denied error. One important correction made during this wave: the FIRST version of startOrchestrationWorker's stub-CLI test double guessed a result shape (result.worker.dispatchId) without checking real output -- the live proof revealed the REAL shape is dispatchId/state/stage at the TOP level, not nested under a worker key. Fixed the stub and its tests to match the confirmed-real shape before any further wiring, rather than building on a guessed contract (exactly the mistake wave 3's own precedent warned against).

waves.summary: Live finding while attempting to resume the parked wave-17 dogfood run through the wave-20-repaired dispatch path: the real Orca CLI rejected task-create with error code consumer_fenced ('This coordinator terminal is bound to run_64fc0fde2aad, not run_5aa5b6d8b029') -- run_64fc0fde2aad was wave 19's disposable proof Run, and this CLI-invoking identity had auto-bound to it and never rebound. Read-only investigation of 'orca skills get orchestration --full' confirmed: a Run is only a durable namespace/inbox, and new orchestration messages/tasks belong to whichever Run the coordinator is CURRENTLY, EXPLICITLY bound to -- reusing a persisted orchestrationRunId from a fresh CLI invocation (exactly TSF's own resume-after-restart scenario) is not automatically safe. `orca orchestration run-use --id <run_id> --json` is the documented rebind command (a plain rebind, not requiring --takeover-legacy, which is for a separate legacy-scheduler-adoption scenario). Manually rebound (run-use --id run_5aa5b6d8b029) to unblock the live resume immediately, then added the proper code fix: bindOrchestrationRun (wraps run-use) in orca-orchestration-bridge.mjs, wired into keep-going-dispatch-loop.mjs's dispatchStep to rebind before reusing an existing orchestrationRunId (skipped when freshly created, since run-create auto-binds). A failed rebind reports DISPATCH_FAILED honestly via the existing commitAbortedDispatch path. This is a genuinely new, previously-unknown Orca coordinator-binding semantic that would have recurred every time the dispatch loop resumes a run from a new process -- not caught by wave 19's proof because that proof always created a fresh (auto-bound) Run. 190/190 full tsf suite GREEN, oxlint/oxfmt/max-lines-ratchet clean.

waves.summary: Independent review of waves 21/22 (commits 0582a91c2/54f4832fc) returned 4 findings; 3 were real, confirmed bugs in the wave-22 placement-collision guard, fixed here: (1) the guard only checked pairs WITHIN one planWave batch, but planWave only separates scope-conflicting items into different batches to keep them off the same files -- it never guarantees batch N+1 waits for batch N to finish, so two items in DIFFERENT batches both defaulting to worktree current still overlapped in the same physical directory, completely undetected; the live dogfood runs own maxConcurrentWorkers:1 config meant the same-batch guard could never fire in production at all, making this cross-batch gap the only real exposure path. Fixed by computing every items placement across the WHOLE wave up front and checking all pairs before any batch is dispatched, refusing the whole wave atomically on a collision. (2) placementsCollide compared worktree/terminal strings with raw strict equality, no path normalization, unlike keep-going.mjs own normalizeScopePath for the analogous scope-conflict check -- two items targeting the same directory via different slash direction or case (a real risk on Windows) went undetected; added a local normalizePlacementPath (lowercase, unify slashes) before comparing. (3) the guard exempted any pair where either side had a terminal set, so it could never catch two items reusing the IDENTICAL existing workerTerminal -- now also flags identical-terminal reuse. Also trimmed bindOrchestrationRuns comment (wave 21) to one line, which wave 22 had already done for a sibling comment but missed this one. Added 3 new tests (cross-batch collision with overlapping-scope items forced into separate batches, identical-terminal-reuse collision, Windows path-variant normalization) and fixed one pre-existing test whose own fixture was itself the exact unsafe pattern the guard now correctly refuses. 198/198 full tsf suite GREEN, oxlint/oxfmt/max-lines-ratchet clean. waves.summary: Closed the verifiers second real finding: keep-going-run-store.mjs's atomicity argument only held within one OS process; data-store.mjs's loadState/saveState have no file lock, no PID check. Added cross-process-file-lock.mjs: a synchronous cross-process mutex using atomic exclusive file creation ('wx', the one primitive genuinely atomic across processes on every supported platform), bounded acquire (10s default, never blocks forever), 30s stale-lock reclaim (mirrors keep-going.mjs's own TICK_LOCK_TIMEOUT_MS reasoning), and a real synchronous sleep between retries via Atomics.wait (not a busy-spin). Wired into withKeepGoingRun, wrapping the load-mutate-save critical section (readKeepGoingRun stays lock-free, matching its existing read-only contract). data-store.mjs gained getStateFilePath() so the lock path derives correctly under the same TSF_UI_STATE_FILE test-isolation override. Manually verified the negative case too (temporarily bypassing the lock, confirming real corruption -- the state file did not even survive -- then reverting), confirming this is a real, serious risk, not theoretical. 205/205 full tsf suite GREEN, oxlint/oxfmt/max-lines-ratchet clean.

waves.summary: Review of waves 26/27 returned 9 findings on cross-process-file-lock.mjs. The most severe (Atomics.wait blocking the ENTIRE Node event loop during lock contention, not just the current request -- turning brief contention into a full-server stall across every project) required redesigning the lock as fully async (setTimeout-based polling, never Atomics.wait), which cascaded: withKeepGoingRun and every keep-going-dispatch-loop.mjs function that touches store.withRun (claim, commitClaimed, every commit* helper) became async, and every call site updated to await. Also fixed from that review: parent directory created before first lock attempt (a fresh install/CI container has no .local-state/ yet -- the prior version threw ENOENT on the first ever Keep Going action); STALE_LOCK_MS (15s) now comfortably below the acquire timeout (30s), since the prior 30s-stale/10s-acquire combination made stale-lock reclaim structurally unreachable; an ownership token written into the lock file so release can never delete a different holders lock (disclosed residual risk: reclaim is still mtime-only, not a liveness heartbeat); Windows EPERM/EACCES/EBUSY retry mirroring the existing plugin-atomic-file-write.ts pattern; an in-process reentrancy guard. WHILE FIXING THE TESTS for this cascade, found and fixed the single most severe bug of this entire session, discovered through my own testing (not a reviewer): the async lock reopened a real timing window where tickKeepGoingRuns own dispatch-vs-settle routing decision (read once, before any lock is acquired) could go stale, letting two near-simultaneous ticks EACH create a genuine, real, duplicate Orca task before either reached its own commit -- reproduced live with direct instrumentation (taskCreateCalls: 2), the exact failure class the concurrency-hardening waves (15b/16/16b) existed to prevent, silently reintroduced by this sessions own async-lock fix for a different problem. Fixed by re-validating the routing decisions assumption (inFlightWave present/absent) against the FRESH, lock-protected read inside claim() itself, rejecting cleanly (TSF_STALE_ROUTING_DECISION) before any orchestration call if stale -- confirmed live afterward (taskCreateCalls back to 1) and covered by a new deterministic regression test using a fake store that simulates the exact race. Also from the review: CONFLICT_CODES now includes TSF_STATE_LOCK_TIMEOUT (409, retryable); the HTTP tick route validates candidate work items before ever reaching tickKeepGoingRun, and dispatchStep itself also now catches a malformed item and releases the tick lock honestly instead of wedging it; the cross-process test now writes a start-time marker per worker process, asserts genuine overlap, and iterates 200x per process instead of 25x. 206/206 full tsf suite GREEN, stable across repeated runs, oxlint/tsc/max-lines-ratchet clean.

gapClassification.gap: Heartbeat projection (mapOrchestrationFacts always emits lastHeartbeatAt: null; detectStall is consequently dead code)
gapClassification.reasoning: Real stall detection already works today via a different, proven mechanism: settleStep's own wall-clock-since-dispatch check, which correctly escalated a genuinely stalled wave to STALLED live this session (waves 17 and 23). The missing heartbeat would be a more precise signal, not a safety gap -- no run can hang indefinitely without detection today. Not required for safe unattended operation.

gapClassification.gap: Lock release-path TOCTOU window (cross-process-file-lock.mjs: readFileSync-then-unlinkSync is not one atomic operation)
gapClassification.reasoning: Requires two independent, narrow conditions to align (this process's release delayed between two syscalls AND another process reclaiming-and-rewriting within that exact gap) against a critical section that is a fast, in-memory-only JSON read/mutate/write with a 15s staleness margin -- disclosed, low-probability, never manifested as a live failure this session across dozens of real lock acquisitions. Worth closing before heavy unattended/cron-triggered use at scale (the cron automation trigger is itself a separate, not-yet-authorized future decision per keep-going-dispatch-loop.mjs's own module header), not before this milestone's adoption.

gapClassification.gap: Per-project lock granularity (one global lock file currently serializes ALL projects' Keep Going operations, not just genuinely racing ones)
gapClassification.reasoning: A scalability/latency characteristic, not a correctness or safety bug -- worst case is bounded added latency (the lock has a timeout) to an unrelated project's request, never data corruption or duplicate dispatch. Only matters once real multi-project concurrent Keep Going load exists, which is not current usage (single active pilot projects). No near-term milestone depends on it.

gapClassification.gap: keep-going-http-routes.mjs's findInvalidWorkItem validates id/scope/worktree-or-terminal but not an allowlist for worktree/agent/spec content -- any local process able to POST to the TSF API (bound to 127.0.0.1 only) could supply an arbitrary worktree/spec
gapClassification.reasoning: This is the standard local-service trust boundary shared by any tool binding to 127.0.0.1 with no auth token -- not a gap introduced by TSF's specific choices, and not exposed beyond localhost. Worth hardening (an auth token, or an explicit allowlist of known-safe worktrees) before this server is ever exposed beyond a single operator's own machine, which is not the current deployment model.

gapClassification.gap: startKeepGoingRun overwrites a prior COMPLETE/BLOCKED run's full history (waves/checkpoints/hash chain) wholesale when a new run starts for the same project, with no separate archive
gapClassification.reasoning: A durability/retention concern across MULTIPLE runs' history over time, not a safety issue within any single run's own execution -- the CURRENT run's own checkpoint chain remains fully intact throughout its lifecycle, satisfying the acceptance criterion's actual wording (checkpoint after meaningful phases within a run). Worth adding a run-history archive before Keep Going sees heavy multi-run-per-project usage, not before this milestone's adoption.

waves.found: A REAL, live bug via genuine HTTP-level integration testing (not just unit tests): POST /api/chat's final saveState call used opState captured once at the very top of the request, before this route's own new dispatch path (chat-dispatch-bridge.mjs's properly-locked withKeepGoingRun writes) could mutate keepGoingRuns. The chat route's own blind saveState({...opState, chatThreads, plannerSessions}) silently reverted a freshly-created Keep Going run back to nothing, the instant the SAME request's own chat-thread-saving code ran afterward. This was harmless before M3 (chat never touched keepGoingRuns), but became a live, reproducible correctness bug the moment dispatch capability existed. Caught specifically because the regression test read the real post-dispatch persisted run state, not just the HTTP response body which looked successful. Fixed by re-reading fresh state right before the final save and merging chatThreads/plannerSessions onto that fresh read instead of the stale snapshot.

A fresh wave was then redispatched for the SAME still-open goal (a genuine Keep-Going continuation after clean recovery, not a duplicate of the fenced worker) -- new real task_673a6b688365 / dispatch ctx_34bf01589433, confirmed dispatched.

TWO real defects found and recorded (both non-blocking for M3 adoption, both real M3/M4 follow-up items, per Tim's explicit instruction): (1) SUPERVISION DEPTH GAP -- the reconciliation loop across waves 11-12 only checked coarse Orca task/worker STATUS fields (which stayed 'dispatched'/'running' throughout the entire 39-minute stall, technically true but uninformative), never the real terminal CONTENT, until this manual reconciliation used orchestration worker-read and found the terminal had gone silent mid-startup. A supervision loop that only checks status, never content, cannot distinguish 'genuinely working' from 'stuck at its own startup' -- this matches the pre-existing, disclosed AGENT_STARTUP_READY-vs-DISPATCH_SUCCEEDED gap already noted in keep-going-dispatch-loop.mjs's settleStep comments, now live-confirmed as a real, reachable failure mode, not merely theoretical. Whether the underlying cause is the same 'dispatch delivery not reaching the session' class of issue recorded in the bedtimeUnattendedMode2026-08-20T01:40 precedent (which that entry notes M2 wave 19/20 already moved away from, using worker-start instead of the older dispatch --inject path) or something else is NOT established here -- recorded as an open question for M4, not a confirmed diagnosis. (2) MONITOR OVERRUN GAP -- two successive session-level Monitor tool calls (30-minute and 15-minute-class timeouts) each silently expired ('killed') without the agent proactively re-arming supervision or reconciling ground truth until Tim manually intervened; the paired ScheduleWakeup fallback (~25 min) should have fired first and forced a real reconciliation but did not visibly do so before Tim's message arrived. Recommendation for M4 (or a targeted M3 follow-up): any live-dispatch supervision loop should (a) periodically inspect real worker-read content once past some fraction of the stall threshold, not just status, and (b) always keep the ScheduleWakeup fallback interval strictly shorter than any armed Monitor's timeout, with each firing performing an explicit real-state reconciliation rather than a no-op re-arm.

Program now switched to WORKDAY_UNATTENDED mode per Tim's explicit instruction: continuing M3 autonomously from this reconciled state, using bounded (<=15min) Monitor windows paired with a strictly-shorter ScheduleWakeup fallback that always reacquires real Orca/TSF truth on every fire (never a silent no-op), checkpointing durable state frequently, never duplicating already-running or settled work, using M2's own stall/retry/NEEDS_YOU mechanisms exclusively, and continuing other non-conflicting program work if a recovery is ever exhausted rather than idling.

waves.summary:
Resolved both wave-1 open design questions with direct source evidence (no guessing, no fixture probe needed -- the source was unambiguous). Q1 YES, confirmed: corrected wave 1's mislabel -- plugin main.mjs modules do NOT run in a worker_thread, they run in a real forked Node child process (src/main/plugins/plugin-host-process.ts's startPluginWorker calls child_process.fork with execArgv:[] and no sandbox/permission flags; plugin-host-runtime.ts is only the message-loop logic running inside that process). Confirmed via plugin-worker-env.ts that the forked process's env is a scrubbed allowlist keeping PATH/HOME/Windows-system-vars but dropping LOCALAPPDATA/ProgramFiles -- a real, minor gotcha for orca-capacity-bridge.mjs's/orca-orchestration-bridge.mjs's own CLI-resolution order (their first 2 candidates would silently miss inside a plugin process; hardcoded-path and bare-orca-on-PATH fallbacks still work). Q2 NO, confirmed and decisive: plugin-panel-controller.ts's load() reads a panel's entry as one text blob wrapped by plugin-panel-shell.ts's buildPluginPanelShellHtml into a sandboxed srcdoc iframe under a hard-coded CSP (default-src 'none'; connect-src 'none'; script-src/style-src 'unsafe-inline' only) -- connect-src 'none' blocks EVERY fetch/XHR call including to a local 127.0.0.1 origin, and script-src 'unsafe-inline'-only blocks loading any separate JS/CSS asset file, so the built multi-file tsf/ui/dist bundle structurally cannot be mounted this way at all. Also confirmed plugin-host-api.ts's PLUGIN_HOST_API_V0 is the complete, authoritative method list (workspace.readContext/terminal.sendText/notifications.show/storage.*/secrets.*/settings.*/events.subscribe) -- no shell.openExternal-equivalent exists, so a plugin cannot even ask the host to open an external URL.

Conclusion: the plugin-panel path is ruled out entirely for hosting the real UI (a deliberate security boundary, not an oversight). The real, viable architecture uses only the plugin's backend process: (1) TSF's existing plugin's activate(orca) spawns tsf/server (extended to serve tsf/ui/dist statically) as a real child process -- confirmed via plugin-service.ts's performRefresh/workerController.reconcile that an approved plugin's worker starts automatically during Orca's own startup reconciliation, not lazily on panel-open, genuinely satisfying 'connects to/starts' with no manual command; (2) since no host API can open a window/URL, the plugin registers a real command (the same orca.commands.register mechanism the current placeholder plugin already uses) that spawns the OS's own url-open process (start/open/xdg-open) when invoked from Orca's command palette; (3) the existing deactivate() export (already supported per plugin-host-runtime.ts) kills the spawned server on shutdown. Updated docs/tsf/M6_DESKTOP_TSF_V1.md with all of this, correcting wave 1's worker_thread mislabel and superseding its 2-candidate open-question framing with one evidence-backed architecture.

First implementation wave: static-file serving of tsf/ui's built SPA, added to the production/standalone path only (tsf/ui's own `npm run dev` is completely untouched -- createRequestHandler's behavior and signature are unchanged). New tsf/server/static-ui-server.mjs exports createStaticUiHandler(distDir): a request whose last path segment has a file extension is treated as a real asset request (404s honestly if missing, never silently serves index.html for a typo'd asset path); anything else falls back to index.html for client-side (react-router-dom) routing. startStandaloneServer(port, options) now accepts an options.uiDistDir override (defaults to tsf/ui/dist next to this module) and serves it via the existing next() fallback in createRequestHandler -- /api/* behavior is completely unchanged.

A REAL bug caught during this wave's own test-writing, not found by inspection: my first path-traversal regression test asserted the wrong thing (expected a plain `../../../../etc/passwd` request to NOT return 200) -- it failed, but investigation showed the URL parser's own dot-segment normalization collapses `..` before the handler ever sees it, so the request safely resolves to `/etc/passwd`, which has no dot in its last segment and correctly falls back to index.html (200, safe SPA behavior, not an escape). Fixed the test to assert the CORRECT expected behavior, and added a second, more meaningful adversarial test using percent-encoded `%2e%2e` (the classic normalize-then-decode bypass vector, since decodeURIComponent runs after URL normalization) against a real sentinel file placed outside distDir -- confirmed the response never contains the sentinel's content. A follow-up mutation-testing spot check (temporarily removing the explicit distDir-escape guard) was inconclusive ON THIS WINDOWS MACHINE specifically -- path.join's own drive-relative-path handling for a leading-slash segment happened to already defeat this exact payload shape here -- but manual reasoning through POSIX path.join semantics confirmed the guard IS load-bearing on Linux/macOS (there, join collapses distDir/../x to the real parent directory), so the guard was restored and documented honestly as platform-dependently redundant-but-required, not removed on the basis of an inconclusive local mutation check.

9 new tests total (7 for static-ui-server.mjs's handler directly against fixture dist directories; 2 integration tests for startStandaloneServer itself, which previously had zero direct test coverage of any kind -- only ever exercised manually, e.g. M4's real restart proof).

waves.summary:
Implemented the real spawn/restart/shutdown lifecycle. New tsf/server/server-process-lifecycle.mjs's startServerLifecycle(options): spawns tsf/server as a real child process, restarts on an unexpected exit with a bounded backoff (never an infinite crash loop, capped at maxRestarts), and treats an EADDRINUSE-shaped stderr message as 'a TSF server is likely already running' rather than a fatal error -- spawnFn/scheduleRestart are injectable so this is unit-tested against a fake EventEmitter-based child process, never a real one (5 tests, including a genuine mutation-testing spot check on the maxRestarts off-by-one boundary, verified by temporarily changing >= to > and confirming the exact expected failure, then restoring). Wired into tsf/main.mjs's activate(): spawns tsf/server (extended with wave 4's static-UI serving) as a real child process for as long as the plugin stays active, satisfying 'connects to/starts required local TSF/Orca services' with no manual command; added a new deactivate() export (already a supported plugin lifecycle hook per wave 2's finding) that stops it cleanly. activate(orca, testOverrides) accepts an optional second argument the real host never passes (plugin-host-runtime.ts calls activate(orca) with exactly one arg) so a real end-to-end test (tsf/test/main-plugin.test.mjs) can exercise a genuine spawn against an ephemeral, randomized port and the real server entry -- confirmed the real child answers real HTTP requests, and confirmed deactivate() genuinely frees the port afterward (not just detaches the handle).

A REAL, significant regression caught only by running the FULL suite (not by running new files in isolation, which passed cleanly and hid the bug): tsf/test/foundation-contracts.test.mjs, a pre-existing file this wave never intended to touch, calls activate() directly to verify command/event registration counts -- with no testOverrides and no corresponding deactivate() call (since deactivate() didn't exist before this wave). Once activate() started spawning a REAL, ref'd child process by default, that pre-existing test's own isolated process (Node's --test-isolation=process spawns one child process per test FILE) never exited -- the live, referenced child-process handle keeps a Node event loop from draining, so the whole full-suite run hung indefinitely (confirmed via real process inspection: an orphaned real tsf/server child and a permanently-alive foundation-contracts.test.mjs runner process, reproduced twice, diagnosed by directly listing live node.exe processes and their command lines via PowerShell/CIM rather than guessing). Fixed by updating that pre-existing test to pass a fake spawnFn (this test's own concern -- command/event registration -- has nothing to do with the server lifecycle, which main-plugin.test.mjs now covers specifically) and to call deactivate() in a finally block. Verified fixed: the two files together now finish in ~460ms (previously hung indefinitely), and the full suite completes in ~6.6s as before, confirmed via a fresh process listing that nothing was left running.

waves.summary: A real, significant portability bug caught during the packaging attempt itself, not by any review: the wave-9 real-proof test (plugin-real-load-proof.test.mjs) depends on `esbuild` to bundle plugin-host-entry.ts/plugin-host-process.ts, but esbuild is not a declared dependency of this project anywhere (only ever an incidental transitive one) -- confirmed the tsf/main worktree (C:/TSF_ORCA) has almost no installed node_modules at all (1 pnpm entry) and genuinely lacks esbuild, causing the whole test file to crash the Node process on the first ff-only-merge re-verification run from that tree. Root-caused and fixed properly rather than papering over it: a literal string `import('esbuild')` gets EAGERLY, SYNCHRONOUSLY resolved by Node's ESM module-linking phase when the target package is wholly absent -- this happens BEFORE the surrounding function body (and any try/catch inside it) ever executes, so no amount of try/catch around a literal-specifier dynamic import can catch it. Confirmed via direct, isolated reproduction (a one-line `node -e` script: `import('esbuild')` inside try/catch still crashes the process; `const pkg='esbuild'; import(pkg)` inside the identical try/catch catches cleanly) that routing the specifier through a variable defeats Node's static pre-resolution and makes a missing esbuild degrade to a normal, catchable promise rejection. Rewrote the test to check availability this way and call `t.skip(...)` with a clear, actionable reason (naming `pnpm install` as the fix) when esbuild isn't resolvable, rather than crashing the whole suite -- the real proof still runs and passes wherever esbuild IS available (re-confirmed in this dev worktree), and gracefully degrades to a skip (not a failure) in a bare checkout without full dev tooling installed, like the actual tsf/main worktree.

waves.summary:
Answered all 4 wave-1 open design questions with hard evidence, and found a genuine, substantial 'false gap' in the process (like M4/M5 found elsewhere). (1) Storage: data-store.mjs is a single flat gitignored JSON file whose DEFAULTS already has 4 per-project maps (chatThreads/plannerSessions/onboardedProjects/keepGoingRuns) -- a new projectMemory:{} key is a straight additive continuation of this exact shape, no new persistence mechanism needed. (2) Provenance: modeled on receipts.mjs's identities/previousReceiptHash pattern and onboarding.mjs's evidence-citation discipline -- every memory record will carry source:{kind,ref,at}. (3) Supersession: keep-going.mjs's replaceGoal (line 125) is a REAL, already-proven mechanism for exactly 'explicit user decisions cannot be silently overwritten' -- authorizedBy!=='TIM' rejected as TSF_GOAL_IMMUTABLE, reason required, old value preserved in an append-only goalHistory[] rather than deleted. Decisions/explicit Preferences reuse this shape; Facts get a looser auto-supersede-but-preserve-history policy (no authorizedBy gate, since they're observational not decisional). (4) Retrieval bound -- THE BIG FINDING: tsf/contracts/project-context-capsule.schema.v1.json already has a do_not_repeat_lessons field, and live-planner.mjs's buildProjectContextCapsule ALREADY returns it as part of the real capsule sent to the real LLM planner call (confirmed via buildSystemPrompt's JSON.stringify(capsule)) -- but hardcoded to [] at line 131, permanently empty, while every sibling array field (completed_missions, active_blockers, approvals, artifacts_created) is already bounded via .slice(). The exact 'no giant transcript injection' retrieval-bound mechanism this milestone needs already exists, is already wired into the real live planner chat path, and just needs to stop being fed an empty array.

Combining this with wave 1's receipts.mjs finding, the real scope narrows further: Decisions likely need NO new storage at all -- only a thin projection over the existing receipt chain (already durable, provenance-aware, and supersession-safe via its own hash chain). The real additive work is: a new pure tsf/domain/project-memory.mjs for Facts and Experiences-Lessons (Preferences folding into Facts with a class discriminator unless a real distinct need appears), a projectMemory:{} key in data-store.mjs, and wiring live-planner.mjs's do_not_repeat_lessons to the new retrieval function instead of a hardcoded empty array. Updated docs/tsf/M7_PROJECT_MEMORY_V2_V1.md with the full findings and revised scope.

Phase 2 of the authorized overnight run (V1 stabilization, not M15): three real V1 failures found and fixed via real evidence, not synthetic cases.

A. Planner Chat authority false positive (server/chat-responder.mjs) -- the same negation/clause-scoping bug class already fixed twice this session in the onboarding classifiers, now fixed in the chat authority gate too, across three independent-review rounds. Round 1: TSF refused an entire read-only readiness-assessment request as TIM_REQUIRED purely because Tim's own prompt listed the consequential actions he was explicitly ruling OUT -- fixed by judging each clause on its own (genuine inquiry/explicit prohibition no longer force TIM_REQUIRED; an unhedged, non-negated directive still does), with "can/could/would/will YOU ...?" kept as a directive (English's own polite-request form). Round 2 (independent review, RED before adoption): splitting only on .!?;\n let an inquiry/prohibition earlier in a comma- or "but"/em-dash-joined run-on sentence exempt a genuine, unrelated directive later in the same loose sentence -- including one reviewer example that silently authorized a destructive repo delete. Fixed by normalizing comma/but/em-dash into hard clause boundaries first. Round 3 (independent review, RED again, narrower): that normalization then let a mid-sentence interjection split a polite "can you ... push this to production?" request away from its own verb+keyword clause. Fixed by checking the polite-request marker against the whole sentence a clause came from (not the post-comma clause fragment), while staying sentence-scoped so an earlier sentence's polite marker never sweeps up a later, unrelated sentence's own prohibition. Independently re-verified GREEN across 43+ constructed phrasings plus cross-sentence leak probing in both directions.

D. Project Health DEGRADED catch-all (server/onboarded-project-projection.mjs) -- HEALTHY_WITH_CAVEATS (no more than a non-blocking caveat: no README, dirty-but-preserved, a linked worktree, a now-resolved handoff discrepancy) was folded into the same DEGRADED fleet-card badge as a genuine NEEDS_ATTENTION finding. A paused/read-only/dirty-preserve project is not inherently unhealthy -- only a real NEEDS_ATTENTION finding reads as DEGRADED now. Underlying findings remain fully visible on the project detail page either way; only the one-word fleet badge changes.

New, found during real NWR + WorldForge overnight readiness analysis (not on Tim's original list, same stabilization pass): the onboarding direction-analysis planner subprocess's "neutral" cwd (tsf/server/.local-state/planner-cwd) was still nested INSIDE this repo, so a real `claude -p` call from it walked up, discovered this repo's own CLAUDE.md (which imports AGENTS.md), and loaded them as its own project instructions -- contaminating the direction/purpose narrative for every onboarded project analyzed. Reproduced live twice independently (both the real NWR and the real WorldForge-Sablewake-Live-Runtime-Repair-V3 direction analyses misidentified the analyzed repo as "TSF Autonomy Program v1" / referenced "the CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md content actually present in this session"). Fixed by rooting the neutral cwd under the OS temp dir instead, outside any git repo's instruction walk-up entirely -- reproduced-then-confirmed-closed via a direct live `claude -p` probe from both the old and new cwd, plus a new regression test that spawns the real invokeLivePlanner path and asserts the actual subprocess cwd is never inside this repo.

waves.summary:
TSF Health Repair Center V1 -- security fixes from independent review round 1 (RED, agent ac0bdb34124e4427b), all confirmed with live exploits by the reviewer and fixed here, all regression-tested.

1. Real shell-injection RCE (server/health-repair.mjs, repo-inspector.mjs discoverCommandGuidance). Only the PREFIX of a package.json script NAME was validated (/^test(:|$)/ matches "test:$(evil)" as happily as "test:unit"), and every consumer of *Commands builds a shell command line by string-concatenating that name -- an attacker-controlled script name became real command execution via the ordinary "Run baseline check" button. Reviewer built a real repo with a malicious script name and got real code execution outside npm's own scope. Fixed at the source: a script name must match a safe identifier shape to be discovered as a runnable command at all. Defense in depth: runBaselineVerification also independently validates the full command line against the exact safe shape discovery is documented to produce before ever spawning it.

2. SENSITIVE authority bypass (server/health-repair-http-routes.mjs /repair and /repair-selected). Both checked only the REQUESTED cause's own repair class, never the project's overall rollup -- an otherwise-safe cause could be auto-repaired on a project that ALSO carries a TIM_REQUIRED cause, directly violating "sensitive projects retain stronger authority... regardless of anything else found." Reviewer onboarded a real project with a committed .env (correctly classified SENSITIVE) and got a real npm install executed via /repair anyway. Fixed: both routes now refuse ANY repair action on a project whose overall diagnosis rollup is TIM_REQUIRED, for any reason, before ever looking at which specific cause was requested.

3. Silent data loss in bulk repair (server/health-repair-http-routes.mjs /repair-selected). No try/catch around the per-project loop, single saveState after the whole batch -- a real exception on project 2 of 3 discarded project 1's already-completed real repair and never attempted project 3. Fixed: each project's repair runs inside its own try/catch and is persisted immediately after it completes.

This is a strong real-world argument for the independent-adversarial-review-before-adoption discipline: these were real, serious, exploitable defects that clean tests/lint/build/typecheck alone did not and could not have caught -- the reviewer had to actually build and run real exploits to find them.

waves.summary: URGENT V1 live-use defect fix: Prepare for Work is now a durable, server-persisted operation (domain/prepare-for-work-operation.mjs, server/prepare-for-work-store.mjs -- same locked CAS pattern as keep-going-run-store.mjs, no new scheduler) instead of one synchronous HTTP request. Root cause: a real bulk WorldForge+NWR attempt chained multiple individually-bounded real sub-operations (live-planner up to ~135s, baseline up to 120s, per project, per selected project) into an emergent unbounded total with no operation identity and no overall bound; the ~9m45s real attempt outlived the TSF desktop host process, and all in-flight progress was silently lost. POST now returns an operation id immediately (202); the pipeline runs detached, persisting per-project phase (RECONCILING/REGISTERING_ORCA/DISCOVERING_BASELINE/RUNNING_BASELINE/DIAGNOSING_HEALTH/REPAIRING_SAFE_CAUSES/VERIFYING/READY_FOR_WORK/NEEDS_YOU/BLOCKED/FAILED) as it goes; GET polls one operation or lists recent ones; server startup automatically reacquires any operation left RUNNING by a crashed prior instance under its own original id, redoing only unsettled projects (every real stage is independently idempotent). Frontend polls with a 30-minute bound instead of holding one fetch open; existing UI components needed no changes. Independent review (3 rounds) found and required fixes for a real lost-update race (prepare-for-work's own onboardedProjects save moved onto the same lock as the new operation store) and an unbounded client poll loop (now bounded). Real acceptance-matrix testing (not the reviewer) found and fixed a real false-READY_FOR_WORK bug: a project whose only remaining causes are all NOT_A_DEFECT (DIRTY_PRESERVE, PAUSED_BY_DESIGN) was reporting READY_FOR_WORK because health-repair.mjs correctly treats those causes as non-defects from a pure health standpoint -- the same class of bug this program already fixed once in the UI's classifyProjectLifecycle, reintroduced one layer down by this fix's new phase field; closed generically per independent review's own recommendation. Real acceptance matrix (isolated preview server): a real 8-project bulk fixture run stayed active 20.2 minutes end to end (crosses both the original ~9m45s window and the required 12 minutes) entirely server-side; a separate real WorldForge+route-reader+quoteloop bulk run was organically interrupted mid-flight by a real process kill and correctly reacquired under the same operation id with zero duplicates, all three projects settling independently; a scripted desktop-restart proof (real process kill + restart mid-BASELINE) confirmed exactly one operation on record afterward. WorldForge: BLOCKED on one real remaining cause (BASELINE_UNKNOWN), repo confirmed unmodified. NWR: BLOCKED on two real remaining causes (BASELINE_UNKNOWN, DEPENDENCY_HEALTH), Orca registration succeeded through the repaired path, repo confirmed unmodified after manual cleanup of a stray package-lock.json written by a pre-existing, separately-disclosed DEPENDENCY_HEALTH gap; NWR's existing canonical-repository identity was not re-litigated. maintenance-loop (clean control): genuine READY_FOR_WORK, zero remaining causes, real typecheck/test/build/lint all passing. route-reader (read-only control): BLOCKED with real mixed causes, never forced into Work Set. quoteloop (DIRTY_PRESERVE negative control): NEEDS_YOU, preserved. Two real, pre-existing, out-of-scope gaps disclosed (not fixed this pass): STALE_PROJECT_STATE's diagnosed trigger (Work Set membership) doesn't match its repair action (REFRESH_ANALYSIS); DEPENDENCY_HEALTH's repair falls back to npm install even for an UNKNOWN package manager.

waves.summary: Fixed a real Tim-reported crash: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading filter) on the Projects bulk-selection/Prepare-for-Work path. Root cause reproduced and confirmed: this program's own wave-27 adoption restarted the real production TSF backend to load the durable Prepare-for-Work operation, but never rebuilt C:/TSF_ORCA/tsf/ui/dist -- the server was serving a pre-wave-27 UI bundle (expects POST /api/projects/prepare-for-work to return {results:[...]} directly) against the new backend (returns {operationId, operation}); BulkActionBar.tsx's result.results.filter(...) throws exactly the reported error when result.results is undefined. Durable fix: prepare-for-work-polling.ts now validates the POST response has a real operationId and every GET poll response is well-formed (including, per independent review's own follow-up finding, each individual settled entry having its own stages array) before use, throwing one clear actionable error instead of crashing; api-response-normalization.ts normalizes portfolio/work/membership-change responses the same way at the API boundary so a missing/wrong-typed array degrades to [] rather than crashing any of the ~10 real consumer call sites across ProjectsPage/HomePage/FleetPage/WorkPage/BulkActionBar. Every change traces to a specific, reproduced cause, not blind optional-chaining. tsf/ui had no test runner at all -- added one using Node's own native TypeScript support (node --experimental-strip-types --test) rather than a new framework; 12 new tests cover the exact reproduced failure and the normalization defaults. Independent review: 2 rounds, GREEN -- confirmed root cause, confirmed the fix closes the reported bug, found and required a fix for one narrow residual (the per-entry stages gap), confirmed complete real-consumer coverage (including WorkPage.tsx, found independently), confirmed the tests are real not tautological, confirmed zero Orca core delta.

waves.summary:
Implemented dependency-aware delivery scheduling. New tsf/domain/delivery-scheduling.mjs: topologicalOrder (Kahn's algorithm, stable input-order tiebreak, throws TSF_WBS_DEPENDENCY_CYCLE honestly on a real cycle rather than guessing an order); computeCriticalPathSchedule -- a deliberately simple, deterministic GREEDY heuristic (not a globally optimal solver -- resource-constrained project scheduling is NP-hard in general, and Tim's own M12 spec explicitly reserves a heavier solver, OR-Tools/CP-SAT as OPTIONAL_SOLVER_BACKEND, for the harder MULTI-PROJECT fleet problem; a single project's own schedule doesn't need that weight). Respects 3 real constraints simultaneously: a task can't start before all its dependencies finish; two conflictsWith-linked tasks never run in an overlapping time window in either direction; at most maxConcurrent tasks are ever in flight at once. Uses each task's EXPECTED hours for one deterministic calendar placement -- overall uncertainty stays reported separately via estimation.mjs's own runMonteCarloEstimate percentiles, a deliberately different question. hourOffsetToDate is a trivial working calendar (configurable hours/day, working weekdays, blackout dates) converting an hour-offset into a real calendar date.
