Bounded remediation only -- no new product capabilities, no Orca fork, Orca core delta stays 0. Closes the one concrete defect M13 found: no real double-click TSF launch experience exists on the machine. Do NOT create M15. CLOSED: Tim performed the final real cold-start acceptance test himself (Orca and Thousand Sunny Fleet both fully closed beforehand, launched via the normal Windows shortcut exactly once, no interaction with Orca/Claude/Codex/plugin settings/Refresh/localhost/a terminal) and it PASSED: the window appeared immediately and reached the real TSF HQ automatically through the proactive activation-nudge path. M14 is complete. Reopened narrowly for wave 9 (a post-acceptance stabilization defect Tim found during real live use -- Orca restarting independently while TSF was open, with no automatic recovery mechanism in place yet) and re-closed after an independent, adversarial review confirmed the fix (an ongoing health check + reuse of the existing bounded recovery sequence) end-to-end, including its own real scratch-server outage/recovery reproduction, separate from this session's own. Per Tim's own framing, this was V1 stabilization discovered during real operator use, not a new feature milestone -- no M15 was created. Reopened narrowly a second time for wave 10 (a post-acceptance live-use defect Tim found and then himself corrected mid-investigation: not TSF minimizing, but Orca repeatedly stealing OS foreground focus -- root-caused to an unconditional `orca open` call on every retry/recovery tick and fixed by gating that call on Orca's own confirmed-running state) and re-closed after an independent, adversarial review re-derived the causal chain from source and ran its own separate live reproduction confirming the fix end-to-end. Per Tim's own framing, this was V1 stabilization discovered during real operator use, not a new feature milestone -- no M15 was created.

waves.summary: Rebuilt tsf/ui/dist from accepted tsf/main source and proved it contains the M9-M12 UI (Fleet Planning, Flight Recorder, regression-check, NO_ESTIMATE_ON_FILE_FOR_PROJECT all present, one match each) -- not the stale M8 bundle it replaces. Full suite re-run clean (588/589, 1 pre-existing skip, 0 failures). Investigated real Orca plugin-settings reactivity (src/main/index.ts) and the safe CLI surface (orca open, orca status --json, fixed TSF_SERVER_PORT=4610) to ground the launcher design. Added tsf/launcher/: Launch-TSF.ps1 (PowerShell, not Node -- a double-clicked launcher cannot assume Tim has Node on PATH), first-run-setup.html (self-contained guided one-time plugin-registration walkthrough, TSF theme tokens, no network dependency), Generate-Icon.ps1 + tsf.ico (TSF-palette shortcut icon, no external asset), Install-/Uninstall-TsfLauncher.ps1 (Desktop + Start Menu .lnk shortcuts, additive-only, never touches Orca settings or any other shortcut). Deliberately did NOT programmatically write to orca-data.json -- the one-time plugin registration stays a Tim-driven guided step through Orca's own existing Settings UI, consistent with Tim's own explicit constraint against silent settings mutation. Real end-to-end verification performed on this machine: installed the real Desktop/Start Menu shortcuts and inspected their properties (correct target/args/icon); ran the real launcher with the plugin genuinely unregistered and confirmed via process list + real window title ("Thousand Sunny Fleet — First-Run Setup") that a genuine dedicated Edge app-mode window opened on the guided setup page after the correct ~30s reachability timeout, logged to %LOCALAPPDATA%\ThousandSunnyFleet\launcher.log; confirmed no leftover Edge child processes tied to the TSF profile after closing the window. Did NOT flip Orca's real pluginSystemEnabled/devPluginPaths settings myself -- that one-time step, and the resulting "reachable" cold-launch proof, is reserved for Tim's own hands-on test per his explicit instruction not to claim that human proof without him.

Independent fork review of wave 1 found 4 real issues, all fixed and re-verified: (1) neither tsf/ui/index.html nor first-run-setup.html declared a favicon, so the dedicated app window would show a generic icon while running, not the TSF mark -- added a matching inline-SVG favicon (same rounded-square/ring/sail design as tsf.ico) to both; (2) Launch-TSF.ps1 built the first-run-setup.html file:// URL by naive slash-flipping with no percent-encoding, so a checkout path containing '#', '?', or spaces could produce a malformed URL and a wrong derived plugin path -- switched to [System.Uri]'s own file-path constructor, confirmed it correctly percent-encodes spaces and '#' (tested directly: 'TSF #2' -> 'TSF%20%232'); (3) the documented ~30s reachability timeout could overrun to ~33-37s because each poll attempt's own 3s HTTP timeout wasn't bounded by the remaining budget -- now caps each attempt to the lesser of 3s and time actually remaining; (4) the design doc named the install/uninstall scripts in lowercase-hyphenated form while the real files are PascalCase -- corrected the doc. Rebuilt tsf/ui/dist and re-ran the full suite clean (589/589, 0 skipped this run). Re-verified the real end-to-end first-run-guide launch after the fixes: correct ~30.1s timeout (down from the unbounded worst case), correct window title, no leftover Edge processes after close.

Tim's own real hands-on acceptance test (plugin registered + enabled + Orca restarted + launcher run) FAILED with 2 reproduced defects. Both diagnosed from real runtime evidence (netstat/Get-CimInstance/CodeIntegrity event log), not by asking Tim to redo setup, and both fixed. DEFECT 1 (plugin enabled but launcher still showed "Checking..."): confirmed via netstat + direct HTTP request that tsf/server was genuinely up and answering 200 on port 4610 the whole time -- the real bug was that tsf/server's JSON responses carried no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, so the first-run guide's fetch() poll (from a file:// origin, Origin: null) had its response silently discarded by CORS in every Chromium-based engine, even though the network request itself completed (which is why every process/port check looked reachable). Fixed with one header on tsf/server's shared json() helper. Reproduced and fixed end-to-end on a scratch port with a real client/server pair: brought up a fixed-code server while a real first-run-guide window was open and polling, confirmed it auto-transitioned to the real UI within one 5s poll cycle, screenshotted. DEFECT 2 (Edge --app felt like a browser wrapper, not a dedicated app): first fix attempt was a compiled, self-contained .NET 8 + WebView2 WinForms host (dotnet publish -r win-x64 --self-contained) -- built and ran cleanly in isolation, but Windows Smart App Control hard-blocked it on the real target machine the instant it tried to launch (Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational event 3077/3118: unsigned executable rejected, no user override once a machine is in enforcement mode). Code signing is both out of scope for this local V1 (Tim's own instruction) and a paid/approval-requiring decision this program does not make unilaterally, so the compiled-exe project (tsf/desktop-host/) was discarded entirely -- never committed. Real fix: Launch-TSF.ps1 now loads the WebView2 SDK's managed net462 assemblies directly into its own already-Microsoft-signed powershell.exe process via Add-Type and hosts a plain WinForms Form + WebView2 control there -- no second executable image is ever loaded, so Smart App Control has nothing new to evaluate. Confirmed empirically: the compiled exe was blocked (event log evidence); the identical control hosted this way was not (no new CodeIntegrity event, real window, real content rendered, screenshotted). Added single-instance handling (named Mutex + FindWindow/SetForegroundWindow) since the window is now this same process rather than a fire-and-forget child spawn. Vendored the 3 required WebView2 SDK files into tsf/launcher/webview2/ (NOTICE.md documents the redistribution license) so no package restore or build step is needed on Tim's machine. Real end-to-end verification on this machine: reachable path (real live backend, real window, correct icon/title, screenshotted), relaunch (second invocation correctly detected the Mutex, activated the existing window, logged it, spawned zero duplicates -- verified via window count), shutdown (closing the window leaves zero orphaned processes, and Orca's own tsf/server -- a separate, Orca-owned process -- is correctly unaffected either way). Full suite re-run: 588/589, 1 failure -- plugin-real-load-proof.test.mjs's own "must not still be listening after shutdown" assertion, which collides with Tim's own real, live tsf/server process legitimately occupying port 4610 for his own ongoing use (the test's own comments anticipate and accept exactly this failure mode). Confirmed via git stash this failure is pre-existing on the unmodified adopted code too -- not a regression from any change in this wave.

Tim's SECOND real hands-on test FAILED: "Orca launched successfully. Thousand Sunny Fleet itself never opened." Diagnosed from a live specimen, not guesswork: a real powershell.exe process from his exact test (matching the shortcut's command line) was found still alive 10+ minutes later, holding the single-instance Mutex, with NO window title and NO WebView2/System.Windows.Forms modules loaded at all -- proof it never reached window creation and had been stuck since very early in the script. Root cause: the wave-3 script ran a synchronous `& orca open --json` call and then an up-to-30s Invoke-WebRequest-based reachability poll BEFORE ever creating any window. Two compounding problems: orca open's own duration on a genuine cold boot is unbounded from the script's point of view, and separately, PowerShell 5.1's Invoke-WebRequest -TimeoutSec does not reliably bound the connection phase against a non-listening loopback port (a known class of issue). Either stalling silently explains the specimen exactly, and -WindowStyle Hidden meant there was no console to ever show an error even if one had been thrown. Fixed structurally, not with a bigger timeout: Launch-TSF.ps1 now creates and shows the dedicated window IMMEDIATELY (measured live: ~0.7-1.1s from double-click), before touching Orca or the network at all. `orca open` is now fired via Start-Process (non-blocking, retried up to 6 times 15s apart in the background -- real recover/retry, not one attempt). ALL reachability waiting moved into first-run-setup.html's own fetch()-based polling (the browser engine's networking stack, not PowerShell's, and not subject to the same quirk), which never gives up on its own: an immediate neutral "Starting Thousand Sunny Fleet..." state, the guided registration steps revealed only past a 20s real-cold-boot-shaped threshold, and an honest "this is taking a while" note past 75s, all while continuing to poll indefinitely and auto-navigating the instant the backend answers. Added a top-level error handler plus a WinForms ThreadException handler so ANY genuine failure anywhere in the sequence shows a real, visible MessageBox -- eliminating the entire silent-death class -WindowStyle Hidden otherwise allows. Verified for real: killed and inspected the actual stuck specimen (confirmed the diagnosis); measured the new immediate window appearance against the live backend; reproduced the full Starting -> (reveal) -> auto-transition sequence end-to-end on a scratch port including bringing a real server up mid-wait; re-verified relaunch (single instance, zero duplicates) and clean shutdown on the new version. Added test/desktop-launcher-cold-start.test.mjs: a structural regression guard (no Windows GUI test harness exists in this repo's CI) that fails if the exact bug shape (a blocking call gating window creation, or a give-up path in the page's poll) is ever reintroduced -- confirmed it genuinely catches the old buggy wave-3 source when pointed at it. Full suite: 594/594, 593 pass, 1 fail (the same pre-existing plugin-real-load-proof.test.mjs port-4610 collision with Tim's own live process, unrelated to this change, previously confirmed via git stash to be pre-existing on unmodified code).

Independent review of wave 4 confirmed the cold-start fix genuinely works (live re-verification on an isolated scratch port/mutex, regression test confirmed to catch the old buggy shape) but found one real, CONFIRMED gap: the top-level try/catch started after the Win32 P/Invoke Add-Type compilation and the Mutex construction, leaving a narrow but genuine window where a cold `Add-Type` compile failure or a restricted Mutex-creation environment could still throw before any window exists, reproducing the exact same silent-death shape this whole fix exists to eliminate. Fixed by moving the try block to wrap everything from the Win32 Add-Type call onward -- single-instance setup, the orca-CLI check, and all window/WebView2 setup are now inside one handler, with the early "already running" / "orca not found" exit paths unaffected (exit does not trigger catch). Re-verified: regression test still passes, live smoke test against the real backend still shows the window in under 1s and clean shutdown, full suite 593/594 (1 known pre-existing port-4610 collision, unrelated).

Tim's third hands-on test was a genuine PARTIAL PASS: cold launch, immediate window, and Orca auto-start all confirmed working -- but with the plugin visibly registered and Enabled, the window stayed on "Still starting..." indefinitely. Diagnosed from the live machine exactly as instructed, without asking Tim to change anything first. netstat/Get-NetTCPConnection confirmed port 4610 genuinely LISTENING with an ESTABLISHED connection from Tim's own real launcher window, and a direct curl -H "Origin: null" confirmed the backend was correctly answering with the CORS header from the earlier fix -- the backend was genuinely reachable. The real question was why activation took so long. Cross-referencing real process-creation timestamps (Get-CimInstance Win32_Process) answered it precisely: every one of Orca’s own subprocesses (GPU, network service, renderer, crashpad handler, parcel watcher, session scanner) started within 5 seconds of Orca’s main process, but the one process that actually runs the TSF plugin (plugin-host-entry.js) did not appear until 4 minutes 23 seconds later, with nothing wrong logged anywhere. Read Orca's own plugin-service source (src/main/plugins/plugin-service.ts, read-only, no core changes) to confirm this is Orca’s own internal activation timing with no supported CLI lever (orca --help and orca status --json’s capabilities both confirmed to have zero plugin-management surface) -- not a bug to fix in tsf/main.mjs or tsf/server, and not something this launcher can make faster without touching Orca core, which stays untouched per this whole program’s constraint. The actual, in-scope defect was the page’s own messaging: first-run-setup.html declared "Orca hasn’t been told where to find Thousand Sunny Fleet yet" as fact after only 20 seconds -- actively misleading on a machine that, like Tim’s, was already correctly configured and simply still activating. Fixed by re-timing the escalation entirely around the real observed delay: a plain "Starting..." for 90 seconds, an honest "this can take a few minutes, nothing to do yet" reassurance from 90s, the registration steps revealed only past 5 minutes and reframed as something to double-check rather than a diagnosis, and a "genuinely unusual" note only past 10 minutes -- all thresholds well beyond the observed 4m23s, enforced by a new regression test that asserts this ordering numerically (and which caught a real off-by-one in this fix’s first draft: an initial 240000ms reveal threshold was still less than the observed 263000ms delay). Also extended Launch-TSF.ps1’s background orca-open retry window (6 attempts/90s -> 24 attempts/6 minutes) as low-cost insurance. Added a second regression test asserting the setup-phase copy never asserts non-registration as fact. Verified live: the readiness poll and CORS fix were unchanged and still correct (confirmed via the same live specimen); an isolated scratch-mutex/port/title copy with shortened thresholds ran for 11 real seconds through all three escalation states with the window remaining Responding=true throughout (no JS/UI-thread crash). Full suite: 596/596, 595 pass, 1 fail (the same pre-existing port-4610 collision with Tim’s own live process, unrelated). Known caveat: while investigating, an early smoke-test command against the REAL shortcut correctly detected Tim’s own window was still open (single-instance Mutex) and activated/refocused it (a benign, content-preserving side effect), and a Remove-Item call ahead of that same test deleted the real %LOCALAPPDATA%\ThousandSunnyFleet\launcher.log before its full diagnostic content had been independently re-verified beyond what had already been read and recorded here -- disclosed rather than hidden.

Independent review of wave 6 found no functional gap in the fix itself (live evidence, process-timestamp gap, and lack of any CLI reconciliation lever were all independently re-confirmed) but flagged one low-severity test-quality issue: the new regression test's negative assertion (!/hasn'?t registered/i) never actually matched the real old buggy copy's wording ("hasn't been told where to find..."), so it was a no-op guard -- the test still correctly distinguished old from new via its sibling positive assertion, so this was never a functional gap in the suite's outcome, but the assertion itself was ineffective. Fixed by broadening the pattern to hasn't (?:been told|registered), confirmed to now genuinely match the real old phrasing. Full suite re-run clean: 596/596, 595 pass, 1 fail (same pre-existing port-4610 collision, unrelated).

Tim's fourth hands-on test again showed the backend genuinely absent (Test-NetConnection failed twice, real evidence) with the plugin visibly Dev . Enabled at the correct path and Orca fully open -- then, mid-diagnosis, reported TSF came up on its own, correlated with using Claude inside Orca. That correlation was the key. REAL ROOT CAUSE, confirmed by reading Orca's own plugin-activation source (read-only, no core changes) and a second live process-timestamp specimen: Orca activates a dev plugin's worker process lazily -- plugin-service.ts's own reconciliation never starts a worker eagerly; the only two call sites that ever call ensure() are invokeCommand() (a command is invoked) and deliverPluginEvent() (a subscribed event fires). TSF's manifest only subscribes to worktree.created/worktree.removed/agent.status.changed, and the last is wired to Orca's real agent-hook pipeline -- it only fires when a real coding-agent session reports status. Using Claude inside Orca is exactly what fired it. A second live specimen confirmed this is not a fixed delay: every Orca subprocess started within 5s this time too, but the TSF plugin-host-entry.js process took 24 minutes 13 seconds to appear -- purely dependent on when Tim happened to trigger one of the 3 events. Deliberate Orca design (do not fork a plugin process until needed), not a bug, not something to change in Orca core. THE REAL FIX: since no CLI/RPC surface exists for plugin management, and fabricating a qualifying event safely was not viable (the only lightweight-looking option, orca worktree create, is a real, heavyweight, highly visible operation -- an inappropriate side effect purely to wake up a plugin), the launcher now invokes TSF's own already-registered, read-only tsf-status command directly against the running Orca instance, using the EXACT SAME local-RPC mechanism every orca CLI command already uses internally: JSON-over-named-pipe, connecting to the pipe named in %APPDATA%\orca\orca-runtime.json and authenticating with the token in that same file (both read-only, both exactly what src/cli/runtime/transport.ts and metadata.ts already do), calling the real plugins.invokeCommand RPC method with {pluginKey: "thousand-sunny-fleet.foundation", commandId: "tsf-status"}. Not a new or unofficial channel -- the identical mechanism orca status/orca open use, just automated instead of typed by a human, triggering the exact same ensure() activation path a real command-palette invocation would. Implemented as a new separate script (Invoke-TsfActivationNudge.ps1) run via Start-Process on the same background retry timer as orca open -- never inline, since NamedPipeClientStream has no reliable ReadTimeout API in classic PowerShell (confirmed empirically: throws "Timeouts are not supported on this stream"), so reads are bounded via Task.Wait(ms) on ReadAsync and the whole attempt via its own wall-clock deadline. Verified for real: ran the raw RPC call directly against the live Orca instance (safe status.get first, then plugins.list confirming exact schema, then the real tsf-status invocation) and confirmed a genuine success response; ran the finished script directly against the real instance (succeeded); ran the full integration through an isolated scratch mutex/window-title/data-dir copy (to avoid touching Tim's real session a third time) and confirmed the nudge fires automatically and succeeds. Did not force a live "not yet active" specimen by deactivating Tim's real working plugin -- ensure()'s idempotent "start-if-not-running, else return existing handle" semantics were confirmed by direct source reading instead (manager.ensureActive(spec)), which is what makes repeatedly invoking tsf-status on every retry tick safe regardless of current state. Added 3 new regression tests: the nudge fires on every retry tick (not just orca open), targets the real plugin key/command/RPC method, and bounds its own runtime rather than relying on the unsupported PipeStream.ReadTimeout. Full suite: 599/599, 598 pass, 1 fail (same pre-existing port-4610 collision with Tim's own live process, unrelated).

Post-acceptance live-use defect found by Tim after M14's own GREEN closure: with TSF's real UI already open and working, the UI suddenly showed the SPA's existing generic "Unavailable -- could not reach the TSF operator API" error. Orca was still open; Tim had not intentionally disabled or removed TSF. Diagnosed as a runtime lifecycle/recovery defect, not a registration/install problem, from real evidence before any fix: real process-creation timestamps showed an entirely new Orca process tree (fresh main process, fresh GPU/network/renderer/crashpad/parcel-watcher/session-scanner subprocesses) -- the OLD Orca session, and everything under it including the old plugin-host/tsf/server, was simply gone. Orca itself had restarted, independent of anything Tim did to TSF, while the TSF window was open. The new session hit the exact same lazy-activation gap wave 8 already fixed, but wave 8's own retry timer is scoped to the initial cold-launch window only and had long since finished -- with no further nudge attempts and nothing else re-checking connectivity, the SPA's generic fetch-failure error was the only thing that ever showed, and its Retry button could never actually help (it only re-fetches; the SPA has no way to reach Orca's plugin activation from inside the web page). Fixed with an ongoing health-check timer (20s interval, runs the whole window's lifetime, not just at launch) that checks reachability via a script executed in the already-loaded page's own context (the browser engine's fetch(), reliable-timeout, not PowerShell's own). On detecting a reachable -> unreachable transition after the real UI had already loaded at least once, it navigates back to the existing first-run-setup.html guide (already polls indefinitely, escalates messaging honestly, has its own Check-again button -- reused as-is) and re-arms the SAME bounded orca-open + activation-nudge retry sequence used at cold launch -- nothing new, same bound, same idempotent nudge, only the ongoing monitoring itself runs for the whole session (cheap, continuous checking, not a retry loop). Found and fixed a real bug during this fix's OWN development: WebView2's ExecuteScriptAsync does NOT await a returned JS promise -- confirmed empirically with a scratch WebView2 window that it always returns the literal text "{}" (the serialized pending Promise) for any promise-returning expression, even a trivial async () => true with no I/O, regardless of Task.Wait, .ContinueWith scheduled on the UI thread, or an Application.DoEvents() message-pumping wait loop. Fixed by having the script report its result via window.chrome.webview.postMessage(...) and listening host-side via WebView2's own WebMessageReceived event -- the correct, documented async round-trip. Verified the complete lifecycle for real, end-to-end, on a fully isolated scratch copy (own Mutex/window-title/data-dir/port, never touching Tim's real session): started a real scratch tsf/server, launched the scratch copy, confirmed it reached the real UI; killed the scratch server outright; confirmed the health check detected the loss (~17-20s later), navigated back to the guide, and re-armed the retry/nudge sequence (all logged); restarted the scratch server; confirmed the guide's own polling detected recovery and auto-navigated the same window straight back to the real UI, fully automatically, zero manual action. Disclosed limitation: recovery re-navigates the whole page, so client-side view state (which tab was open) is not preserved across an outage -- the actual operator data (projects, Work Set, Keep Going runs, all server-persisted) is never touched by this mechanism. Added 4 new regression tests: the health-check timer never has a bounded give-up (only stops at window close); the result is read via postMessage, never ExecuteScriptAsync's return value; recovery only triggers after a real prior connection while the real UI was showing; recovery re-arms the existing bounded retry sequence, never a new unbounded one. Full suite: 603/603, 602 pass, 1 fail (same pre-existing port-4610 collision with Tim's own live process, unrelated).

Post-acceptance live-use defect found by Tim after wave 9's own closure: the TSF window kept appearing to fall behind another window roughly every ~30 seconds. Tim himself corrected the initial framing after watching more closely -- TSF's own window never actually minimized; a brief Windows loading spinner appeared, then Orca suddenly jumped to the foreground in front of whatever app he was using. The investigation target was changed from "TSF minimizes" to "Orca steals foreground focus" per Tim's own instruction, and the prior retry-timer-unbounded hypothesis (pursued before the correction, including three faithful isolated reproductions) was abandoned once a careful recount of the real launcher.log showed the retry timer actually stopping cleanly at its 24-attempt bound both times it ran -- an earlier miscount, not a real defect. Root cause, confirmed from source and a live reproduction: Launch-TSF.ps1's retry-tick handler called `orca open --json` via Start-Process unconditionally, every ~15s for up to 24 attempts, both at cold launch and on every backend-loss recovery cycle, regardless of whether Orca was already running and healthy. Orca's own CLI (src/cli/runtime/client.ts's openOrca(), read-only, no core changes) calls launchOrcaApp() -- which re-spawns the Orca executable -- before checking desktopWindowStatus, not after; the already-running Orca's own Electron single-instance handling (src/main/index.ts's requestDesktopActivation -> focusExistingWindow, wrapping src/main/window/focus-existing-window.ts) then answers that redundant relaunch by force-focusing its own window (app.focus({steal:true}), window.show()/.focus(), and on win32 moveTop()/an always-on-top pulse/a 100ms focus retry) -- entirely unrelated to TSF's own window, which this never touches, explaining exactly why TSF never appeared to minimize. Confirmed live: a single manual `orca open --json` call while Orca was already running and focused elsewhere caused the OS foreground owner to flip to Orca's real pid within ~1-2 seconds (measured via a read-only GetForegroundWindow/GetWindowThreadProcessId poll), with zero effect on TSF's own IsIconic state; Tim independently observed the exact steal happen in real time when this reproduction was run. Fixed by moving the "launch Orca if it isn't running" decision into Invoke-TsfActivationNudge.ps1, gated on Orca's own runtime metadata pointing at a still-live pid (Get-Process -Id) -- orca open now only fires when Orca is genuinely not confirmed running; the pre-existing RPC-based plugin-activation nudge (zero window/focus side effects) still runs unconditionally every tick, so backend-loss recovery keeps working even when Orca itself never went down. Launch-TSF.ps1's own retry-tick handler no longer references orca open or the resolved orca executable at all. Verified live on three isolated scratch copies (Tim's real running specimen never touched): zero "launched it" log lines while Orca was confirmed running across all three, and a clean, fully hands-off run (no Claude-Code background-task-wait mechanism involved) showed zero foreground-to-Orca transitions across a complete retry cycle -- two earlier runs had shown one late spurious transition each, traced to this session's own background-task-wait tooling causing an unrelated, legitimate Orca surface event, ruled out as a false lead once a run without that tooling showed none. Added two new regression tests: the retry-tick handler no longer calls orca open directly, and the nudge script's orca-open launch is gated behind the confirmed-running check while the RPC nudge stays unconditional. Full suite: 605 tests, 604 pass, 1 skip, 0 failures.

gaps: Tim's fourth hands-on test surfaced the real root cause (Orca's lazy dev-plugin activation) and this wave adds a genuine functional fix (an activation nudge over Orca's own real runtime RPC), independently reviewed with maximal adversarial scrutiny given its novelty (a hand-rolled named-pipe RPC client). Both the review and this session verified the mechanism directly against the real live Orca instance (safe, read-only, idempotent tsf-status invocations only). Tim's own confirmation that a real cold start now reaches the UI quickly (seconds, not minutes) rather than depending on incidental agent activity remains his to give.
No packaged/signed installer -- explicitly out of scope for this local V1 per Tim's own instruction.

Low-severity, non-blocking (per independent review of wave 8): an abandoned ReadAsync Task on a timeout in Invoke-TsfActivationNudge.ps1 is never explicitly re-observed before pipe disposal -- confirmed harmless by .NET behavior (no crash on unobserved task exceptions) and scoped to a disposable helper process even in the worst case; accepted as-is.
Low-severity, non-blocking (per wave-3 review): FindWindow(null, "Thousand Sunny Fleet") has a theoretical, negligible risk of matching an unrelated window sharing this exact title -- accepted as-is.

reVerifiedFromMergedTree.realShortcutsRepointed: Install-TsfLauncher.ps1 re-run from C:/TSF_ORCA/tsf/launcher (the adopted tree)
reVerifiedFromMergedTree.realSmokeTest: Not re-run through the real shortcut this cycle by this session, to avoid a further unnecessary touch of Tim's own live window/log. The independent review of this exact commit DID run the real, unmodified Invoke-TsfActivationNudge.ps1 directly against the live Orca instance (disclosed: this appended one benign success line to the real %LOCALAPPDATA%\ThousandSunnyFleet\launcher.log, no deletion, no window/Mutex touch) and separately verified the full Launch-TSF.ps1 integration through a fully isolated scratch copy -- both succeeded.

adoptionReceipt.rootCauseAndFix: Tim's fourth real hands-on test showed the backend genuinely absent (Test-NetConnection failed twice) with the plugin visibly Dev . Enabled at the correct path and Orca fully running -- then, mid-diagnosis, the backend came up on its own, correlated with using Claude inside Orca. Root cause, confirmed by reading Orca's own plugin-activation source (read-only) and independently re-confirmed by the review: Orca activates a dev plugin's worker lazily -- only via invokeCommand() or delivery of one of its subscribed events, and TSF's agent.status.changed subscription is wired to a real agent-hook pipeline that only fires from genuine agent activity. A second live specimen showed this delay can reach 24+ minutes, purely dependent on incidental Orca activity -- deliberate Orca design, not a bug. Fix: the launcher now proactively invokes TSF's own already-registered, read-only tsf-status command directly against the running Orca instance, using the exact same local RPC mechanism every orca CLI command already uses internally (JSON-over-named-pipe, real plugins.invokeCommand method) -- not a new or unofficial channel, the same one orca status/orca open already use.
adoptionReceipt.independentReview: A maximally adversarial fork review (justified by this wave's novelty -- the first hand-rolled RPC client in this program) independently re-derived the entire diagnosis from Orca's own source, confirmed the RPC wire-protocol implementation is a faithful match against the server's real validation logic, ran its own live RPC calls and the real nudge script against the actual running instance, constructed real mutations in scratch copies to confirm all 3 new regression tests genuinely fail without the fix, and confirmed full suite/core-delta results independently. Two low-severity findings filed, both non-blocking and accepted as-is (recorded above).

wave10StabilizationReview.rootCause: Launch-TSF.ps1's retry-tick handler called `orca open --json` unconditionally on every tick (cold launch and every backend-loss recovery cycle), regardless of whether Orca was already running. Orca's own openOrca() CLI implementation calls launchOrcaApp() (re-spawns the Orca executable) before checking whether a desktop window is already available. The already-running Orca's Electron single-instance handling answers that redundant relaunch by force-focusing its own window (app.focus({steal:true}) plus moveTop()/an always-on-top pulse/a 100ms focus retry on win32) -- never touching TSF's own window, which is why TSF never appeared to minimize even though Tim's first-pass observation suggested it had.
wave10StabilizationReview.fix: Moved the "launch Orca if it isn't running" decision into Invoke-TsfActivationNudge.ps1, gated on Orca's own runtime metadata (%APPDATA%\orca\orca-runtime.json) pointing at a still-live pid, confirmed via Get-Process -Id. orca open now only fires when Orca is genuinely not confirmed running. The RPC-based plugin-activation nudge (plugins.invokeCommand over the named pipe, zero window/focus effects) still runs unconditionally every tick as before, so backend-loss recovery keeps working even when Orca itself never went down. Launch-TSF.ps1's retry-tick handler no longer references orca open or the resolved orca executable at all.
